newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, China oppose monopoly in world leadership.
newsitem.headline: Russia, China oppose monopoly in world leadership.

text.p: The presidents of Russia and China on Tuesday joined forces in opposing the domination of one superpower in the post-Cold War world in a declaration which the Kremlin described as a breakthrough in its Asian policy.

"One may talk about a breakthrough in Russian policy in Asia," Itar-Tass news agency quoted President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying after the Kremlin leader's talks with the Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
The two leaders crowned their summit by signing a declaration "On the multi-polar world" which outlined their joint vision of the world order in the next century.
"No country should seek hegemony, practise power politics or monopolize international affairs," the Chinese official Xinhua news agency quoted the declaration as saying.

"Someone is longing for a single-polar world. He wants to decide things himself," Yeltsin, 66, standing next to the smiling Jiang, 70, told a brief news conference after the signing. Yeltsin, who had heart surgery last year, looked stiff and grim but fully in control.

Officials from Russia and China, both of which have problems with the West and are jealous of claims by the United States to be the sole superpower in the post-Cold War world, said the declaration was not aimed against any specific country.
"The very suggestion of plans to create some counter-blocs are wrong and counter-productive," Interfax news agency quoted Yastrzhembsky as saying.
Jiang, Yeltsin and the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan will on Thursday sign a treaty on reducing armed forces along the former Soviet-Chinese border.

Few details of the treaty have been made public. Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev's spokesman said on Tuesday that the five states would reduce their forces deployed near the border and pull them back 100 km (60 miles).
But Interfax quoted a Russian foreign ministry official as saying that the treaty did not envisage pulling back troops.

"The agreement does not provide for any troop withdrawal but rather concerns control over their numbers," the official said, adding that the treaty would simply make the 100 km strip transparent for checks and thus remove mutual suspicions.
China and Russia have made clear that they want their political declaration and the five-way treaty to set an expample to other countries on how to maintain regional stability.

Yastrzhembsky also made clear that talks with Jiang were part of Moscow's search for new allies which could diversify its foreign policy, focused mainly on the West after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

He said that Yeltsin, talking to Jiang, expressed his satisfaction with "the positive developments in a 'triangle' of China-Russia-India". Indian Prime Minister H.D.Deve Gowda visited Moscow in March.
Yeltsin said he and Jiang also managed to solve a number of problems which had hindered the development of bilateral ties.
"We have discussed more than 20 issues with the Chinese partners including border problems, the number of forces deployed along our common border and nuclear energy," he said.

Later on Wednesday Jiang addressed the communist-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament and met its chairman, Gennady Seleznyov. He was due to meet the leader of the Federation Council upper house Yegor Stroyev later in the day.
Yeltsin and Jiang will meet for more talks on Thursday when the Chinese leader will also meet Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

Jiang, who knows Russia's language and literature, will on Friday visit Yasnaya Polyana, the estate of 19th century writer and philosopher Leo Tolstoy about 200 km (130 miles) south of Moscow. He will leave Moscow on Saturday.
